title: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling
claim: Correcting exposure bias at early sampling steps yields sharper intermediate predictions and higher-quality final outputs than a baseline matched on compute.
layout: 2 regions: left 3 trajectory rows, right 3x2 paired grid; blue arrows
description: The figure has two regions. On the left are three horizontal rows of five or six image frames. They are labeled Original Trajectory, NFE-Matched Trajectory and PEEK Trajectory. Each row shows a denoising path from a gray noisy blob to a clear picture of an orange barrel beside green plants, with tiny sigma labels under each frame. The PEEK row is visibly sharper and more colorful in its early frames. On the right is a grid of paired final samples, in three rows and two column pairs. Each pair is headed NFE-Matched then PEEK, joined by a curved blue arrow. The samples include a blue gate, a goldfish, a tower, a white van, a building door and a greenhouse. The PEEK samples show finer detail. The eye goes first to the left trajectory rows.
caption: PEEK performs a provisional one-step update, and uses the look-ahead prediction to interpolate the current prediction at selected positions. The selected clean prediction is then used to construct the next noisy state. The trajectories illustrate that the early-step predictions tend to be especially low-quality, and PEEK can yield higher-quality images. Best viewed in color.
abstract: Diffusion image generators owe much of their practical success to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. However, during sampling, the denoiser predicts the next step from flawed inputs that differ substantially from real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry images, missing details, or distorted shapes). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates the current clean prediction with this one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more image like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule with a greedy metric-driven search made efficient by the PEEK prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. Across pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings on CIFAR-10, LSUNBedroom,I mageNet, and MS-COCO,the look-ahead correction consistently improves over baselines matched by number of function evaluations (NFE), with FrÃ©chet Inception Distance (FID) reductions up to 49.3%. The one-time per-model calibration, the only extra cost, takes at most 2.2 minutes in our experiments. Project website is available at https://dachengruoque.github.io/PEEK-Video/.
